chapter_title: CloudFront with Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions

screens.title: CloudFront with Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions
screens.subtitle: Run small, focused compute at the CDN edge to shape requests and responses with millisecond impact.

narration.text: Edge compute lets you run code close to your users to change requests or responses before they reach origin servers. In this chapter you will learn two CloudFront-native options: Lambda@Edge, which brings Lambda to CloudFront events and supports more complex logic and network calls, and CloudFront Functions, which runs tiny JavaScript snippets in the point of presence for ultra-low latency operations. We’ll show the event types that trigger edge code, concrete patterns such as A/B testing, URL rewrites and header injection, and the operational trade-offs like execution limits, memory, and cost. You will also see practical code examples and a hands-on activity to deploy a URL-rewrite function. By the end you’ll be able to pick the right edge compute tool for a given task and avoid common mistakes such as over-engineering, forgetting limits, or misconfiguring permissions. Think about a real site you manage: how much of its logic could safely move to the edge to reduce origin load and latency?

keyIdea.title: Run targeted logic at the CDN edge
keyIdea.text: Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions let you inspect and modify requests and responses at CloudFront locations, enabling personalization, routing and security before traffic reaches your origin.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Overview

CloudFront edge compute options

Use the edge to personalize content, reduce origin load, and apply security rules with JavaScript that runs earlier in the request lifecycle.

Lambda@Edge
Regional Lambda extended to run at edge events. Suited for complex logic and network calls.
CloudFront Functions
Tiny JavaScript running in the PoP for sub-millisecond transforms and header changes.
Why choose one?
Trade latency, cost, and capability: network calls and longer runtime favor Lambda@Edge; scale and latency favor Functions.
In this lesson: you will inspect event types, limits, code examples and a short lab to implement a URL rewrite with a CloudFront Function.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Module 11
Visual: request flows through CloudFront. Lightweight functions run inside the PoP; Lambda@Edge runs regionally close to PoPs and can reach network resources.
Explore Key Topics
Event types and triggers
Viewer/Origin request and response events determine when code runs.
When to use each service
Match latency, scale and network needs to the service limits.
Practical patterns
A/B testing, URL rewrites, header injection and access control at the edge.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide practice and assessment for edge compute in CloudFront. First, you will be able to explain what Lambda@Edge can do, including the four CloudFront event types and when to use regional Lambda capabilities at the edge. Second, you will learn to compare Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions precisely, weighing factors like execution time, memory, and whether network calls are required. Third, you will implement common edge patterns: A/B testing, URL rewrites and header manipulation, using the appropriate event triggers. Fourth, you will write, deploy and test simple JavaScript functions for CloudFront Functions and understand the deployment and permission steps needed for Lambda@Edge. Each objective contains a short practical mnemonic so you can recall which tool to choose: complexity, latency, network access and deployment constraints. By the end you should be able to pick the correct edge compute pattern for a feature request and avoid common operational mistakes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Operational Skills
screens.subtitle: Deploy, test, and manage edge functions safely

narration.text: Beyond knowing what edge functions can do, you will learn the operational skills that make deployments safe and reliable. This includes deploying Lambda@Edge functions to the required region and publishing CloudFront Functions to distributions; configuring IAM permissions to allow logging and necessary AWS calls; and using CloudWatch and CloudFront real-time logs to debug behavior. You will also practice testing in the console and with synthetic events before publishing. Finally, you will learn to analyze invocation costs and monitor for high-request counts to avoid surprises. These operational competencies reduce risk when moving logic to the edge and help you troubleshoot limits or latency that show up only under load. As you proceed, consider what monitoring and rollback steps you would add to a production deployment to keep user experience stable. Learning Objectives — Operational Skills means deploy in the right region, give correct permissions, and use logs and tests to validate edge function behavior before and after publishing.. In practical terms, deploy, test, and manage edge functions safely. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Operational Objectives
Deploy and Permissions
  • Deploy Lambda@Edge in the required region so CloudFront can replicate it globally.
  • Assign IAM logs permissions to allow CloudWatch reporting and troubleshooting.
  • Publish CloudFront Functions via the console and associate with distribution behaviors.
Testing and Observability
  • Use the function "Test" feature for CloudFront Functions and CloudWatch logs for Lambda@Edge.
  • Monitor invocation counts and latency to track cost and performance.
  • Plan rollbacks and staged publishes for low risk releases.
Cost Awareness
Edge functions are billed per invocation. CloudFront Functions are cheaper per request. Anticipate high traffic and calculate costs for frequent invocations before moving logic to the edge.
Common Operational Pitfalls
  • Forgetting to publish a CloudFront Function after editing.
  • Using Lambda@Edge for trivial tasks that a Function can handle.
  • Not monitoring invocation spikes which increase cost quickly.

screens.title: Edge compute: why run logic at CloudFront?
screens.subtitle: How executing code at the CDN reduces latency and origin load

narration.text: Edge compute moves small amounts of logic to the CDN so requests and responses can be modified without a round trip to the origin. That matters because even small latency gains at the edge reduce page load time for global users and lower origin request volumes, which saves cost and improves scalability. Typical operations at the edge are routing decisions, URL canonicalization, header injection for security, or quick access control checks. A concrete example: instead of sending every request to an S3 origin to decide which index file to return, a CloudFront Function can rewrite '/products' to '/products/index. html' in sub-millisecond time. A common misconception is that every server-side task should be moved to the edge. In reality, stateful work or heavy payload processing belongs at the origin or in regional services because edge functions are stateless and limited in runtime and memory. When planning migration to the edge, list the operations that are idempotent, stateless, and small in scope. Those are the safest candidates. To check your understanding, identify one request-modifying task in your app and consider whether it needs network access or longer processing; if not, it is a good edge candidate.

keyIdea.title: Move small, stateless logic to the edge
keyIdea.text: Use edge functions to reduce latency and origin load for operations that are fast, stateless, and do not require external network calls.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Edge Compute Rationale
Definition

Edge compute runs code at CloudFront locations to inspect and mutate requests and responses before they traverse the network to origin servers.

Latency: sub-millisecond opportunities for critical request handling.
Origin load: fewer requests to back-end services and lower bandwidth.
User experience: faster first meaningful paint through early rewrites and routing.
Concrete example: URL rewrite

A CloudFront Function can canonicalize '/about' to '/about/index.html', saving an origin lookup and avoiding a redirect response. This improves latency and reduces origin hits.

Misconception
Not every task belongs at the edge. Heavy computation and stateful work should stay at origin or regional services.
Try this
Pick a simple request transform in your app and estimate whether it needs network access; if it doesn't, consider moving it to a CloudFront Function.

screens.title: CloudFront event types that trigger edge logic
screens.subtitle: Viewer and Origin events, and how they map to use cases

narration.text: CloudFront invokes edge code at four distinct points in the request and response lifecycle. Understanding these events determines whether logic runs before the origin sees a request or after the origin has responded. Viewer Request runs as soon as CloudFront receives a request from a viewer; use it for URL rewrites, A/B test routing decisions, header checks, or custom authentication that must deny access quickly. Origin Request runs when CloudFront forwards a request to the origin; it’s useful to add origin-specific headers or transform requests before a backend sees them. Origin Response runs after the origin returns a response but before CloudFront caches it; you can normalize status codes, modify body or headers before caching, or set custom cache keys. Viewer Response is the last chance to change the response sent to the user, ideal for injecting small client scripts, or adding security headers to responses that came from cache. A common misconception is that all events have identical capabilities; event choice affects latency, caching, and whether you can set cookies from the function. For practice, map three features—authentication, A/B test routing, and response header injection—to the event you would choose and why.

keyIdea.title: Pick the right event
keyIdea.text: Viewer events alter incoming requests early; origin events let you change what the backend sees or modify responses before caching.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Event Types
Viewer Request
Trigger at the moment CloudFront gets a viewer request. Use for URL rewrites, redirects, A/B routing and early auth checks that must block before origin access.
Origin Request
Modify a request before it reaches origin, for example adding origin authentication headers or transforming image paths for the backend.
Origin Response
Run after the origin returns a response and before caching. Great to normalize status codes, add cache-aware headers or modify responses prior to cache storage.
Viewer Response
Final chance to change headers or small content before CloudFront serves the client. Useful for last-mile personalization or security headers on served content.
Example mapping
Authentication that must run before origin: Viewer Request. A/B split based on cookie: Viewer Request. Add security header to cached responses: Origin Response or Viewer Response.
Misconception
Not every event can set cookies to the viewer. Some cookie-setting patterns require response events to persist a variant selection.
Check
When you need to change what the origin sees, prefer Origin Request. When you need to alter cached content, use Origin Response.

screens.title: Lambda@Edge: capabilities and limits
screens.subtitle: Runtimes, execution time, memory and network access

narration.text: Lambda@Edge extends AWS Lambda to run in response to CloudFront events globally. It supports more complex logic than a CloudFront Function because Lambda@Edge can run Node. js or Python, make network calls, and access larger memory within defined limits. Key limits are important: viewer events generally have a short maximum execution time of five seconds, while origin events can run up to thirty seconds. The memory limit is 128 megabytes for many edge-triggered Lambdas, and functions execute in AWS regions closest to the edge location that handled the event. That regional execution matters because functions may access other AWS resources or external APIs and so latency to those resources is a factor. Deployment rules require that the function be created in a specific region for replication and association with distributions. A common misconception is that Lambda@Edge functions are identical to regular Lambda in every way; edge functions have stricter cold-start, packaging, and replication behaviors you must design for. When you need external A P I calls or more complex processing, Lambda@Edge is the appropriate choice, but be mindful of time and memory constraints when writing your handler.

keyIdea.title: Lambda@Edge for complex, networked logic
keyIdea.text: Use Lambda@Edge when you need external calls or heavier processing, but design for its execution time and memory limits.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Lambda@Edge
Capabilities
  • Runs Node.js or Python logic at edge-triggered events.
  • Can make network calls and access other AWS services.
  • Suitable for external authentication checks, payload transforms, and heavier processing within limits.
Limits and deployment
Viewer events: up to 5 seconds. Origin events: up to 30 seconds. Memory commonly limited to 128 MB for edge functions. Functions must be deployed in the required replication region for CloudFront.
Practical note
Design for short execution and avoid blocking long-running network calls. Use retries and timeouts when calling external services.
Example
An OAuth check that needs an HTTP call should be implemented in Lambda@Edge at Viewer Request to block unauthenticated requests early.
Misconception
Lambda@Edge is not a full replacement for regional backends. It is optimized for short, network-capable tasks but still has stricter limits than standard Lambda in some contexts.
Takeaway
If your logic needs network calls or more work than a tiny JS snippet, prefer Lambda@Edge and design for its time and memory constraints.

screens.title: CloudFront Functions: design and constraints
screens.subtitle: Why Functions are faster, cheaper, and more limited

narration.text: CloudFront Functions are purpose-built for ultra-low-latency transformations that must run at the point of presence. They execute within the PoP with sub-millisecond execution times and support only JavaScript. The trade-off is strict limits: a maximum execution time around one millisecond, memory limited to about two megabytes, and no network access or external resource calls. These constraints make Functions ideal for URL canonicalization, simple header additions, IP-based access control, and high-scale A/B splits where you need to handle millions of requests with very low cost. A common misconception is that Functions can replace Lambda@Edge for anything; they cannot make HTTP requests and cannot perform large payload manipulation. A concrete example is enforcing trailing slashes: a Function can append 'index. html' to a URI quickly without touching the origin. When deciding, test your logic against the Function limits and prefer CloudFront Functions when the operation is tiny, stateless, and does not require external data. CloudFront Functions: design and constraints means choose cloudfront functions when you need minimal processing, maximum throughput, and no network access.. In practical terms, why functions are faster, cheaper, and more limited. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Functions for tiny, high-scale tasks
keyIdea.text: Choose CloudFront Functions when you need minimal processing, maximum throughput, and no network access.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › CloudFront Functions
What they are

Tiny JavaScript functions that execute at CloudFront PoPs with extremely low latency. Designed for simple request/response modifications at very high scale.

Execution time: ~1 ms
Memory limit: ~2 MB
No network access
Ideal use cases
  • URL rewrites and redirects for canonicalization.
  • Security headers on viewer response.
  • A/B routing based on cookies or simple random split.
Misconception
They are not a drop-in replacement for Lambda@Edge when network calls or larger processing are required.

screens.title: Lambda@Edge A/B testing example
screens.subtitle: Inspect cookies, assign variants, and rewrite the URI

narration.text: A common edge pattern is A/B testing: decide which variant to serve and rewrite the request so the origin receives the variant path. The Lambda@Edge example provided inspects cookies to find an existing variant, assigns a random variant if none exists, and rewrites the request URI for the chosen variant. This handler runs at Viewer Request so the routing happens before origin access. The code demonstrates reading request headers, parsing cookies, and setting request. uri for variant B. Note that setting a persistent cookie usually happens in a response event; this function demonstrates the routing decision itself. A misconception is expecting viewer request functions to set persistent cookies on their own; persistent cookies require a response to the viewer or origin to instruct the client. In practice, combine a Viewer Request routing function with a Viewer Response or Origin Response that adds a Set-Cookie header to persist the choice. This walkthrough shows the request-side routing logic you will use to serve different content versions without additional redirection. Lambda@Edge A/B testing example means inspect cookies or assign variants and rewrite the request uri so the origin receives a variant-specific path; use response events to persist cookies.. In practical terms, inspect cookies, assign variants, and rewrite the uri. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use Lambda@Edge for server-side A/B routing
keyIdea.text: Inspect cookies or assign variants and rewrite the request URI so the origin receives a variant-specific path; use response events to persist cookies.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › A/B Testing (Lambda@Edge)
Lambda@Edge Handler (Viewer Request)
exports.handler = async (event) => {
  const request = event.Records[0].cf.request;
  const headers = request.headers;

  // Default variant
  let abTestVariant = 'A';

  // Check for an A/B test cookie
  if (headers.cookie) {
    for (let i = 0; i < headers.cookie.length; i++) {
      if (headers.cookie[i].value.includes('abtest=B')) {
        abTestVariant = 'B';
        break;
      }
    }
  }

  // If no cookie, randomly assign
  if (!headers.cookie || !headers.cookie.some(c => c.value.includes('abtest='))) {
    if (Math.random() < 0.5) {
      abTestVariant = 'B';
    }
    // To persist the variant, add Set-Cookie in a response trigger.
  }

  if (abTestVariant === 'B') {
    request.uri = '/variantB' + request.uri;
  }

  return request;
};
Concrete detail
Routing happens before origin fetch. Persisting variant requires setting cookie in a response event.
Key Takeaway

Separate routing (request event) and persistence (response event) when implementing A/B tests at the edge.

screens.title: CloudFront Function: URL rewrite example
screens.subtitle: A tiny JavaScript function that canonicalizes directory requests

narration.text: CloudFront Functions are ideal for URI canonicalization because they run extremely fast and have low cost per request. The example function inspects the request. uri and appends 'index. html' when a URI ends with a slash or lacks a file extension. This is a pure transformation that doesn't need network access, making it a perfect candidate for a CloudFront Function. Important execution considerations include keeping logic minimal to stay within the one millisecond limit and avoiding heavy parsing. A common mistake is adding synchronous operations that increase runtime or trying to call external services from a CloudFront Function; such calls are forbidden. When you publish this function and associate it with the Viewer Request event on a behavior, CloudFront will execute this transformation on every matching request. Test locally using the function console test events and with representative URIs to ensure rule coverage. Consider edge cases like query strings and prefixed paths when writing your tests. CloudFront Function: URL rewrite example means use cloudfront functions to canonicalize uris like '/products' to '/products/index.html' to remove round trips to the origin.. In practical terms, a tiny javascript function that canonicalizes directory requests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Rewrite without origin cost
keyIdea.text: Use CloudFront Functions to canonicalize URIs like '/products' to '/products/index.html' to remove round trips to the origin.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › URL Rewrite (CloudFront Function)
CloudFront Function (Viewer Request)
function handler(event) {
  var request = event.request;
  var uri = request.uri;

  // Check whether the URI is missing a file extension.
  if (uri.endsWith('/')) {
    request.uri += 'index.html';
  } else if (!uri.includes('.')) {
    // Handles /products -> /products/index.html
    request.uri += '/index.html';
  }
  return request;
}
Check your tests
Test URIs with and without trailing slashes, and with query strings, to ensure consistent mapping to index.html.
Try
Publish the function and associate it to Viewer Request for a behavior that serves static site content, then test in console with sample events.

screens.title: CloudFront Function: add security headers
screens.subtitle: Inject Strict-Transport-Security and other headers on Viewer Response

narration.text: Adding security headers at the edge is a common and efficient use of CloudFront Functions because it avoids modifying origin servers and guarantees consistent headers for cached responses. The sample Viewer Response handler adds Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options and X-Frame-Options to the response. headers object. This pattern is simple, stateless, and does not require network access, making it well-suited for CloudFront Functions. A common mistake is trying to mutate headers in an unsupported way or assuming headers will be present; always code defensively by checking the response object. Also remember that cache behavior may cause these headers to be cached along with the response; if different headers are required per viewer, consider where to set them and how caching keys influence behavior. Test the function in the CloudFront console and verify responses from both cache-hit and cache-miss scenarios to confirm consistent header injection. CloudFront Function: add security headers means use viewer response cloudfront functions to ensure security headers are applied uniformly to cached and uncached responses.. In practical terms, inject strict-transport-security and other headers on viewer response. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Consistent security headers with minimal cost
keyIdea.text: Use Viewer Response CloudFront Functions to ensure security headers are applied uniformly to cached and uncached responses.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Security Headers
Viewer Response CloudFront Function
function handler(event) {
  var response = event.response;
  var headers = response.headers;

  // Add Strict-Transport-Security header
  headers['strict-transport-security'] = { value: 'max-age=63072000; includeSubdomains; preload' };
  // Add X-Content-Type-Options header
  headers['x-content-type-options'] = { value: 'nosniff' };
  // Add X-Frame-Options header
  headers['x-frame-options'] = { value: 'SAMEORIGIN' };

  return response;
}
Practical tip
Confirm headers are present for cached responses as well as for misses; caching may preserve headers you inject.
Common mistake
Attempting to perform heavy transformations or external calls in a Function. Keep it short and deterministic.

screens.title: Choosing between Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions
screens.subtitle: Match capabilities to requirements and cost considerations

narration.text: Choosing the right edge compute option starts with requirements: does your logic need network access or extended processing time? If yes, Lambda@Edge fits because it supports Node. js or Python, network calls, and origin event types. If your requirement is simple, extremely latency-sensitive transformation at scale, CloudFront Functions is preferable because of sub-millisecond execution, minimal memory usage, and lower cost per invocation. Cost implications are important: CloudFront Functions are charged at a lower per-invocation price and scale very well for large traffic volumes. Lambda@Edge incurs higher per-invocation costs and additional considerations like replication and regional deployment. A common pitfall is over-engineering: avoid choosing Lambda@Edge for a trivial rewrite that a Function can handle. Another pitfall is ignoring limits—CloudFront Functions cannot make network calls and have very small memory budgets, so any attempt to call an A P I will fail. Use a two-column comparison of execution environment, languages, time limits, memory, network access and typical use cases to make an informed decision for each feature request. Choosing between Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions means match required capabilities—network access, runtime, execution time—to the service. prefer cloudfront functions for tiny, high-scale tasks and lambda@edge for more complex work.. In practical terms, match capabilities to requirements and cost considerations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Right tool for the job
keyIdea.text: Match required capabilities—network access, runtime, execution time—to the service. Prefer CloudFront Functions for tiny, high-scale tasks and Lambda@Edge for more complex work.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Service Comparison
CloudFront Functions
  • Run in PoP, sub-millisecond latency.
  • JavaScript only, ~1 ms limit, ~2 MB memory, no network access.
  • Best for URL rewrites, headers, IP checks, A/B splits at scale.
Lambda@Edge
  • Runs in regions closest to PoP, supports Node.js and Python.
  • Execution time up to 5s (viewer) or 30s (origin), network calls allowed, memory limits apply.
  • Best for authentication checks calling external APIs or heavy transforms.
Cost
CloudFront Functions are cheaper per invocation. For very high traffic, cost favors Functions for simple logic.
Scale
Functions excel at massive request volumes due to minimal overhead; Lambda@Edge scales but with higher cost and replication behavior.
Decision checklist
Ask: Do I need network calls? Is the logic tiny and stateless? Will this run at very high volume? Use checklist to select service.

screens.title: Deployment, testing and monitoring edge functions
screens.subtitle: Publish, test with console events, enable logs and monitor costs

narration.text: Deployment and operation of edge functions require specific steps to ensure safety. For CloudFront Functions, author the JavaScript in the console, use the built-in Test feature to validate with synthetic viewer request or response events, then Publish the function and associate it with a distribution behavior at the desired event type. For Lambda@Edge, create and deploy the function in the required region so CloudFront can replicate it globally; ensure IAM permissions allow writing logs. Testing is critical: use CloudWatch Logs for Lambda@Edge to inspect runtime behavior and use CloudFront’s real-time logs to observe traffic patterns. Monitor invocation counts, errors, and latency because cost is per invocation. Set alerts for spikes to avoid unexpected bills. A common operational mistake is forgetting to publish or associate the function after editing, or not validating behavior under cache-hit and cache-miss scenarios. To practice, run the URL rewrite function in test mode for both '/about' and '/about? lang=fr' and verify you get the expected rewritten URI in the output. Deployment, testing and monitoring edge functions means use console testing, cloudwatch, and cloudfront logs to validate behavior and monitor invocation volumes to control cost and reliability.. In practical terms, publish, test with console events, enable logs and monitor costs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Test and observe before production
keyIdea.text: Use console testing, CloudWatch, and CloudFront logs to validate behavior and monitor invocation volumes to control cost and reliability.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Deploy & Monitor
Deployment steps
  1. Author and test function in console.
  2. Publish CloudFront Functions; associate with distribution behaviors.
  3. For Lambda@Edge, deploy in required region and grant logging permissions.
Testing & Monitoring
  • Use the function Test feature for representative events.
  • Enable CloudWatch logs for Lambda@Edge and inspect real-time CloudFront logs for traffic patterns.
  • Track invocation counts and errors to manage cost and reliability.
Pitfall
Not verifying behavior during cache hits can hide header or rewrite issues. Test both cache-hit and cache-miss cases.

screens.title: Common mistakes and best practices
screens.subtitle: Avoid over-engineering, respect limits, and manage state correctly

narration.text: When adopting edge functions, teams often make predictable mistakes that increase cost or break behavior under load. One frequent error is over-engineering: using Lambda@Edge for trivial rewrites or header changes that CloudFront Functions handle cheaper and faster. Another is ignoring limits—writing functions that exceed runtime or memory budgets will fail in production. Incorrect IAM permissions are also common; Lambda@Edge needs logging permissions to write CloudWatch entries, and missing permissions hide runtime failures. State management at the edge is a third challenge: edge functions are stateless, so rely on cookies, query parameters, or an external store accessed by Lambda@Edge (not CloudFront Functions) when state is essential. Best practices include: choose the least capable service that still meets requirements, test with realistic traffic and cache scenarios, add observability and alerting for invocation spikes, and document where state lives. A short checklist before deploying: confirm event type, ensure no network calls in Functions, run console tests, publish and monitor logs. Which of these best practices could you apply first to a new edge feature in your application? Common mistakes and best practices means prefer the simplest service that meets requirements, test limits, and plan state management deliberately to avoid failures and unexpected costs.. In practical terms, avoid over-engineering, respect limits, and manage state correctly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical guardrails
keyIdea.text: Prefer the simplest service that meets requirements, test limits, and plan state management deliberately to avoid failures and unexpected costs.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Mistakes & Practices
Avoid over-engineering
If a task is a simple header change or URI rewrite, prefer CloudFront Functions over Lambda@Edge to reduce cost and latency.
Respect limits
Design for 1 ms/2 MB for Functions and 5–30s for Lambda@Edge. Validate under expected traffic to avoid unexpected failures.
State management
Edge functions are stateless. Use cookies or an external datastore (via Lambda@Edge when needed) to manage session-like data.
Checklist
  • Confirm event type meets requirement.
  • Check for network calls—Functions can’t make them.
  • Publish and monitor invocation metrics and logs.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Summarizing the chapter: Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions let you run JavaScript at CloudFront to inspect and modify traffic. Lambda@Edge is suited for more complex logic, supports Node. js or Python, and can make network calls. CloudFront Functions are extremely low latency, JavaScript-only, and cannot access external resources. Remember the four CloudFront event types—Viewer Request, Origin Request, Origin Response, and Viewer Response—each serving different use cases and placement in the request lifecycle. Core patterns include A/B testing, URL rewrites, header manipulation, and simple access control. Finally, operationally, test functions in the console, publish carefully, ensure correct IAM permissions for Lambda@Edge, and monitor invocation counts to manage cost. Keep this checklist in mind as you decide whether to move logic to the edge. Key Concepts means use cloudfront functions for tiny, high-throughput transforms and lambda@edge for complex, networked tasks; pick the event that aligns with when you must run logic.. In practical terms, what to remember from this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Key Concepts
Lambda@Edge
Regionally executed Lambda with network access for complex edge logic.
CloudFront Functions
Tiny JS in the PoP for ultra-low latency, no network calls and strict limits.
Event types
Viewer Request, Origin Request, Origin Response, Viewer Response define when you can run logic.
Summary Takeaway
Choose the least-powerful service that meets your needs, test under realistic scenarios, and instrument logs and metrics to manage cost and reliability.

narration.text: Keep these essential terms in mind: Viewer Request occurs when CloudFront receives a client request; Origin Request triggers before the origin fetch; Origin Response runs after origin returns and before caching; Viewer Response runs just before the content is returned to the viewer. A/B testing, URL rewrites and header manipulation are frequent edge use cases. Remember that CloudFront Functions are best for tiny, stateless operations at scale, while Lambda@Edge supports network calls and heavier transforms but costs more and has deployment considerations. Final advice: test, publish, observe logs, and design for stateless operations at the edge. keyIdea.title: Four events and two services
keyIdea.text: Remember the four CloudFront events and match them to either CloudFront Functions for tiny transforms or Lambda@Edge for networked logic.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Remember
Viewer Request
Earliest trigger for routing and early auth.
Origin Events
Modify requests to origin or responses before caching.
Use cases
A/B testing, rewrites, headers, access control – pick the right event and service.
Final Tip
Start with small, well-tested Functions for trivial transforms and reserve Lambda@Edge for tasks that must call external services or perform non-trivial computation.

ai_generation_note: Create a 10-minute animated explainer video comparing Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions. Show simple code snippets for each (e.g., a header modification for CloudFront Functions, an external API call for Lambda@Edge). Use clear diagrams to illustrate the flow of a request through CloudFront and where each function type executes. The tone should be informative and concise. Include an interactive element where users drag and drop use cases (e.g., "complex authentication," "simple URL rewrite") to the correct service.
